title: Discover a reproducible breakdown of general relativity near black holes

concept.text: The innovation would be an independently reproducible observation showing that general relativity fails to describe gravity near a black hole, with the departure specified quantitatively. Its defining achievement would be evidence that the theory reaches a physical limit in strong gravity. Sharper images, more precise measurements or observations that agree with the theory would improve the available tests without completing this discovery.

One proposed route is to measure the geometry of a black hole’s narrow photon ring and compare it with predictions for a Kerr black hole. The June 2024 Black Hole Explorer (BHEX) study proposes measurements around M87* and Sgr A*. Such measurements could connect observable ring structure to strong-field geometry, but a discrepancy with a Kerr-model prediction would require further interpretation: it could implicate assumptions about the source or measurement rather than general relativity itself.

significance.text: A demonstrated failure of general relativity near black holes would expose an empirical boundary of a foundational physical theory. The supplied BHEX study grounds this possibility in a concrete observational goal: comparing photon-ring geometry with general-relativistic predictions. The revolutionary significance is conditional on establishing that a measured departure actually concerns gravity, after plausible astrophysical and instrumental explanations have been tested.

As a conditional scientific consequence, a characterized departure would give successor theories something quantitative to explain, including where and by how much existing predictions fail. It could help discriminate among explanations if those explanations make different predictions for subsequent observations. Discovery would not automatically supply a successor theory, establish a particular account of quantum gravity or show that general relativity fails outside the conditions actually tested.

The direct advance would belong to observational astronomy and gravitational physics. Space interferometry, photon-ring detection and improved reconstruction could enable it, but the impact of those technologies must be distinguished from the impact of finding new physics. Successful measurements that remain consistent with general relativity would still constrain alternatives and strengthen empirical knowledge of strong gravity.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is to isolate a reproducible geometric departure strongly enough to attribute it to a failure of general relativity. Detecting a narrow feature is only part of that task. The supplied review reports that the BHEX paper discusses transient plasma structures that can mimic photon-ring features, residual dependence on source emission and the effects of instrumental noise. These complications make it necessary to establish what physical structure an observation actually measures before using it to infer spacetime geometry.

The abstract describes photon-ring shape as largely insensitive to the precise emission details, while the reviewed full-text discussion retains astrophysical dependence for the first subring. These statements support a promising geometric probe, not a completely source-independent measurement. The engineering and inference challenge is to obtain sufficient resolving capability and signal quality while controlling the remaining ambiguity between geometry, emission and noise.

Proposed evidentiary safeguards include independent calibration and reconstruction checks, explicit uncertainty estimates, tests of alternative source models and repetition with independent observations. The supplied evidence supports the plasma, emission and noise concerns; it does not establish the specific extent to which calibration or reconstruction errors can imitate a spacetime departure. Those checks remain justified components of a proposed demonstration rather than documented explanations of an observed anomaly.

current_state.text: The supplied review identifies the BHEX study, submitted on 13 June 2024, as a proposal to measure narrow photon rings around M87* and Sgr A* and use their geometry to test Kerr predictions. Its abstract describes the thin ring as unresolved at that time. This is a dated proposed experiment and scientific testing route, not a report of a detected violation of general relativity. The supplied materials do not establish a subsequent achieved measurement or the proposal’s peer-review status.

The reconciled research cites an Event Horizon Telescope release dated 22 January 2025 as reporting a persistent luminous ring around M87* consistent with the expected shadow scale. That observational claim remains unverified within the supplied evidence because no artifact of the EHT page was retained. The missing artifact does not establish that the claim is false, and the BHEX proposal cannot substitute for evidence of this later result. A broad luminous ring and a resolved narrow photon ring must also remain distinct observational achievements.

The supplied review used an identified arXiv abstract and a partially extracted paper covering pages 1–25. PDF extraction skipped some form content, and the figures were not visually inspected. These limitations permit the reported textual conclusions about the proposal and its caveats, but do not support claims of complete inspection or independent validation of its figures. The supplied freshness search record is empty, so these materials do not establish the field’s status as of 1 November 2026. No demonstrated breakdown of general relativity is documented in this evidence set.

completion_criteria.text: A proposed convincing demonstration would specify the observable departure and its magnitude, then establish that departure through independent observations of one or more black holes. The analysis should account for astrophysical and instrumental uncertainties, test competing explanations and show that the result survives credible changes in data analysis. These are proposed completion criteria for this concept, not thresholds prescribed by the supplied paper or established community standards.

completion_criteria.text: The inference must also test the premises connecting the observation to the predicted signal. A failed Kerr-model fit alone would be insufficient: the investigators would need to show why source emission, transient plasma structures, noise or other assumptions underlying the comparison cannot adequately explain the discrepancy. The reviewed BHEX study supplies the geometric testing goal and concrete reasons to examine these alternatives, but does not report that this evidentiary task has been completed.

completion_criteria.text: Further proposed requirements are reproducible analysis and predictions that succeed on observations beyond those used to formulate the explanation. Independent measurements should recover a consistent quantitative departure under comparable conditions; any dependence on the target or observing conditions should be explained and tested. The final claim should state its practical boundaries, including which objects and physical regimes were examined. Finite observations could demonstrate a breakdown over that tested domain without establishing its behavior near every black hole.
completion_criteria.label: Further proposed requirements are reproducible analysis and predictions

related_concepts.text: AST-10, “Open the millihertz gravitational-wave sky as a working observatory,” overlaps through the possibility of observing black-hole systems and testing gravity with a different kind of signal. Its defining achievement is an operational observing capability; AST-07 requires a reproducible failure of general relativity. AST-05, “Detect and identify a primordial gravitational-wave background,” likewise concerns gravitational observations, but targets an early-universe signal rather than a breakdown near black holes. These are conceptual distinctions drawn from the supplied roster, not claims that either concept has been achieved.

AST-13, “Establish how the earliest massive black holes formed and grew,” shares black holes as its subject. Understanding their formation and growth could improve astrophysical context, while a confirmed change to gravity could affect some models of their evolution. Neither outcome establishes the other: a formation history does not demonstrate a failure of general relativity, and a local strong-gravity departure does not by itself explain the earliest massive black holes.

AST-03, “Identify the physical constituent of astronomical dark matter,” and AST-04, “Establish the physical cause of cosmic acceleration,” also seek explanations for foundational astronomical phenomena. A departure near black holes might constrain broader gravitational explanations, but it would not automatically identify dark matter or establish the cause of cosmic acceleration. Their distinct physical targets and required evidence remain separate.

AST-08, “Produce resolved surface maps of rocky exoplanets,” and AST-06, “Map the cosmic dark ages and first luminous structures in three dimensions,” share the broad challenge of extracting spatial information from difficult astronomical observations. Their desired outputs are maps of particular targets. For AST-07, improved spatial information is an enabling measurement whose significance depends on what it establishes about gravity; producing a more detailed image alone does not satisfy the concept.

change_log.reason: These reviewed details explain both the promise and limitations of photon-ring geometry as a strong-gravity probe.

unresolved_issues: The cited EHT release’s identity, contents and claimed persistent ring consistent with the expected shadow scale remain unverified within the supplied materials.
The empty freshness search record leaves the field’s status as of 1 November 2026 unestablished.
The BHEX paper’s peer-review status and subsequent experimental progress are not established by the supplied evidence.
Skipped PDF form content and uninspected figures limit completeness of the supplied review.
The specific effects of calibration and image reconstruction on an apparent spacetime departure are not established by the retained evidence.
No supplied evidence settles what quantitative uncertainty, replication breadth or predictive success would be sufficient to attribute an observed departure to general relativity itself.
